clue.text: Spooner's spouse mined rock in enclosed space

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of the two words change places

parts.note: hubby is an informal word for a husband, a spouse
coal is the rock dug from mines, said aloud like 'cole'

explanation.surface: A husband dug out stone in a confined space, as told by the Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hubby coal' with its opening sounds swapped by 'Spooner's' becomes 'cubby hole'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cubbyhole is a small snug room or compartment, an enclosed space.

clue.text: Fish nearly all bone

parts.note: the carp is a freshwater fish

indicators.note: nearly means the word falls one letter short, its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: A fish that is practically nothing but bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' trims all to AL. The answer is an adjective used as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpal is any of the small bones of the wrist.

clue.text: A loner at odds with this warrior code might be dishonourable

indicators.note: things at odds are in disagreement and out of order, so letters must be rearranged
the combined letters could become another word when rearranged, so a composite rearrangement is signalled

parts.note: the full word the combined letters make
these letters are taken away from the longer word

explanation.surface: A lone samurai who breaks the code of honour could be called disgraceful.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: A LONER plus the answer can be rearranged into DISHONOURABLE, so take ALONER out of DISHONOURABLE and rearrange the remaining DISHOUB.
explanation.definitionFit: Bushido is the Japanese samurai ethic of loyalty and honour, the traditional code of conduct for fighting men.

clue.text: Liverpudlian hit scared soldier after advance

parts.note: yellow means cowardly
a sub is an advance on wages
a marine is a soldier serving at sea

explanation.surface: A frightened soldier from Liverpool strikes out after moving forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After advance' puts the soldier behind the advance. A sub is British slang for money paid ahead of payday.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beatles came from Liverpool, and this 1966 single of theirs topped the charts, so it is a Merseyside band's chart success.

clue.text: Love great character of Greek

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
mega is slang for great

explanation.surface: Someone adores a fine personality from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in the surface, but here it means a letter of an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, and a letter is a written character.

clue.text: Kitchen utensil for one consumer outside this land

indicators.note: to sit outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: e.g. means for example, for one
an eater consumes food
GB, Great Britain, is the setter's own country

explanation.surface: A cooking gadget suited to a shopper living abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This land' means the country the British setter writes in, Great Britain, abbreviated GB; EG and EATER together go outside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg beater is a whisk with rotating blades, a hand-held tool used in cooking to whip eggs.

clue.text: Problem acquiring credit for struggling people

indicators.note: to acquire is to take in, so one piece gains another within it

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: A difficulty in getting a loan for those who are hard up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struggling people' looks like the poor needing credit, but it describes a jostling crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrum is a disorderly crowd of people pushing and shoving, as in the rugby formation where forwards grapple for the ball.

clue.text: Helper for training group in bar role regularly in tears

indicators.note: in only sets the group alongside the bar, following it

parts.note: a spar is a pole or bar
a ring is a group, as of conspirators or dealers
a part is a role in a play

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the words that follow

parts.note: the words in tears, whose alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: Someone in a pub, playing a part, keeps bursting into tears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'in tears': N, E, R.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparring partner is the person a boxer practises with, someone who helps with training.

clue.text: About finished? Gather together

parts.note: round means about, as in 'round the house'
'time's up' means time is finished

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a job is nearly done, then calls everyone together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About finished?' reads as a question asking whether something is nearly done, but each word is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To round up is a phrasal verb for collecting scattered people or animals into one place, like cattle.

clue.text: Graduate high-flier rebuffed the old claptrap

parts.note: an MA is a Master of Arts graduate
a lark is a bird that soars high while singing

indicators.note: to rebuff is to push back, so the letters are sent back the other way

parts.note: ye is an archaic form of 'the'

explanation.surface: A high-achieving graduate brushed off the outdated nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-flier' suggests a star pupil but is a bird; 'Ye olde' shows YE as an old spelling of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Malarkey is informal for nonsense or empty talk, the same meaning as claptrap, insincere or foolish speech.

clue.text: Doggedness making comeback, European victor defeated opponent

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the string runs back the opposite way

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the opponent who was beaten

explanation.surface: A tenacious sporting comeback in which a European champion beats a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' looks like a winner in the sporting story but is just V from the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolve as a noun means firm determination, the same quality as stubborn persistence or tenacity.

clue.text: Progressive bhangra Dua Lipa sampled

indicators.note: in music sampling lifts a snippet from a track, so a short stretch is lifted from the words

parts.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: Pop star Dua Lipa borrowed from forward-thinking Punjabi dance music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Progressive' looks like a genre label for the bhangra, but it is the definition; the answer spans bhanGRA DUA Lipa.
explanation.definitionFit: Something progressive happens step by step over time, which is what gradual change means.

clue.text: Do you see me as work friend?

parts.note: the question 'am I ...?' asks how someone views you
to work is to function or go

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a colleague regards them as a friend at the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work friend' looks like one phrase for a colleague, but 'work' ends the question 'am I go?' and 'friend' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is Spanish for friend and is widely used in English as a casual word for a pal.

clue.text: Teen that spies beer I'm unsure should nab ten free

indicators.note: to nab is to grab and hold, so the outer pieces take others into their midst

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
er is the sound of hesitation
X is the Roman numeral for ten
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: An adolescent peeping at a beer worries whether to grab ten for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Alex Rider is Anthony Horowitz's teenage spy in a popular series of children's novels; 'spies' is part of the definition, not wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Alex Rider is a fictional schoolboy recruited by MI6, so he is a young secret agent in the novels.

clue.text: Work within firm in the French city formerly

indicators.note: within means inside, so one piece is placed inside the others

parts.note: constant means steadfast, firm
taken as written
le is French for 'the'
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Employment inside a company based in a French city in times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' goes inside everything else, just before the French article. 'Formerly' belongs to the definition, since the city is now Istanbul.
explanation.definitionFit: Constantinople was the earlier name of Istanbul until the twentieth century, so it is a place under an old name.

clue.text: Trouble first of nurses in room adjoining hospital department for dressing

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble

indicators.note: placing something in another puts it inside

parts.note: RM is the abbreviation for room

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the initial letter
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A problem with the leading nurse in a room next to the ward where wounds are bandaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' suggests a wound dressing in the hospital scene, but it means decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressing can mean decoration, as in window dressing, and an adornment is an ornament that embellishes.

clue.text: Storyteller's book is at separate points held in censure

indicators.note: being held inside something at two different places means the pieces are inserted apart from each other

parts.note: to fault is to criticise or censure
B is the abbreviation for book
taken as written

explanation.surface: A narrator's volume is criticised in various places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At separate points' means B and IS go into FAULT at two different places, FA-B-UL-IS-T; the 's after the definition stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fabulist is a teller of fables, and by extension a liar who invents tales, so a teller of stories.

clue.text: Maybe self-publicist's euphoria to brag outrageously

indicators.note: acting outrageously is wild and out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: fourteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A show-off's delight in boasting shamelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-publicist' normally means a shameless promoter; with 'Maybe' it becomes someone who literally publishes their own life story.
explanation.definitionFit: An autobiographer writes and releases a book about their own life, punningly making them a self-publicist.

clue.text: Friar with greed, perhaps, eats heartily

parts.note: Friar Tuck is Robin Hood's companion
greed is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: A gluttonous monk digs into his food with gusto.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Tuck is the jolly, food-loving monk in the Robin Hood legends.
explanation.definitionFit: To tuck in is a British idiom meaning to start eating a meal with enthusiasm and appetite.

clue.text: Take home captivating article made of clay

indicators.note: to captivate literally means to hold captive, so one piece imprisons another inside it

parts.note: to earn is to take home as pay
'the' is the definite article

explanation.surface: Bringing back a charming piece of pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take home' suggests carrying something home, but it means earning a wage, as in take-home pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthen describes pots or floors formed from baked soil or clay, so it is an adjective for that material.

clue.text: Banks in Portugal limit security

indicators.note: banks are the edges of a river, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters
an edge is a limit or border

explanation.surface: Lisbon's banks cap the guarantee they offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like financial institutions, matching 'security', but it means the edges of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A pledge is something handed over as a guarantee for a loan, which is what security means in finance.

clue.text: Loose tea covered by university study that has been retracted

indicators.note: something covered by another is enclosed by it

parts.note: uni is short for university
cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: retracting is drawing back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a den is a study or private room

explanation.surface: A university research paper on loose-leaf tea has been withdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose tea' reads as one phrase, but 'Loose' is the definition and 'study' is a room, not research.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unchained has been released from its fetters, so it is free or at liberty.

clue.text: Be successful after clipping fastening

indicators.note: clipping trims the last letter off the phrase

parts.note: to do well is to be successful

explanation.surface: Someone makes a success of things once the fasteners are snipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after clipping' cuts the end letter off DO WELL.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowel is a wooden peg that holds two pieces together, a type of fastening.

clue.text: Country's king before unframed paintings

definitions.note: the definition is the adjective form: country here means rural, as in country life

indicators.note: the king comes before the other letters

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: unframed takes away the edge letters, the frame of the word

parts.note: murals are paintings done on walls

explanation.surface: A nation's monarch stands in front of paintings stripped from their frames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unframed' strips MURALS of its first and last letters, leaving URAL. 'Country's' reads as a possessive but is the definition, the adjectival sense of country.
explanation.definitionFit: Rural means of the countryside, as country does in phrases like country life.

clue.text: Pensioner is confused, erasing one's novel for Kindle

indicators.note: confused things are muddled, so the letters are mixed up
novel means new, so what remains takes on a fresh arrangement
to erase is to rub out, so some letters are removed

parts.note: the letters before removal
these letters are rubbed out

explanation.surface: A bewildered old person wipes their novel off an e-reader.
explanation.walkthrough: Take O, N, E and S out of PENSIONERIS and rearrange what remains. 'Kindle' is not the e-reader but a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To kindle enthusiasm or feeling is to arouse it, which is what inspiring someone does.

clue.text: Used machine to hoist as revolutionary parts turn

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, so one piece is inserted

parts.note: to wind is to turn a handle
Che Guevara, the Argentine revolutionary

explanation.surface: Lifting with a machine while rotating parts spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary parts' suggests rotating machine parts, but 'revolutionary' is Che and 'parts' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To winch is to haul up with a winding drum and cable, so winched means lifted by such a device.

clue.text: Colour covered by rust, in general

indicators.note: something covered by words lies concealed within them

parts.note: letters running across the words

explanation.surface: A shade generally obscured by corrosion.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across rusT IN GEneral, ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinge is a faint trace of a hue, and to colour is to tint, so both name a slight shading.

clue.text: Indulgence of treacle on bananas

indicators.note: going bananas is slang for going crazy, so the letters run wild

parts.note: nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A sweet treat of syrup poured over banana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like part of a dessert with treacle, but it is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Indulgence can mean leniency toward others' faults, which is what tolerance means: patient forbearance.
